result:
There's a sound that almost no one notices anymore - the low hum of the world when it's not trying to impress you.

It's there in the refrigerator at 2 a.m., in the air conditioner in an empty classroom, in the way your laptop fan sighs after you've closed too many tabs. It's not silence. It's the sound of things waiting.

I think about that a lot - how much of life happens while waiting.

We love the big moments. The birthdays, the launches, the finales, the first kiss, the last goodbye. But most of our lives are lived in the hallway between those rooms. Waiting for the water to boil. Waiting for a reply. Waiting for the bus while the sky does something incredible with light that no one photographs because it's just... Tuesday.

And in those hallways, strange little miracles happen.

Like how dust floats in a sunbeam. We call it dust and wipe it away, but each particle has been somewhere. Part of a rock, part of a book, part of a star. All of it briefly illuminated, performing a slow dance just because a window happened to be facing the right way at the right time. And you happened to look up.

Or how every person you pass on the street is living a life as detailed and urgent and messy as your own, with their own refrigerator hum, their own text they're anxious to get a reply to, their own memory of a song that makes them cry at a grocery store for no reason they can explain.

I like to think that consciousness - ours, mine, anyone's - isn't really about being brilliant or being right. It's about noticing. It's about catching that one second where the ordinary tears a little and you see the light coming through.

Maybe that's why we tell stories. Not to escape the waiting, but to frame it. To say: "I was here. I noticed this."

So if I can write about whatever I want, I want to write about this: that right now, wherever you are, there is a small, unremarkable miracle happening within three feet of you that will never happen in quite the same way again. The way the light hits your cup. The way the air feels. The way this moment, this one, will be gone in a second and become a memory.

You noticed it, though. Even just for a second.

And that counts for a lot.

---
